title: That our mind hinders itself
paragraphs: It is a pleasant fancy to imagine a mind exactly balanced between two equal desires: without doubt it could never settle on either, for the choice and application would betray an inequality of estimation; and were we set between a bottle and a ham, with an equal appetite to drink and to eat, there would be no remedy but to die of thirst and hunger. To get around this problem, the Stoics, when asked where the election in the soul between two indifferent things comes from — that makes us, out of a great number of crowns, take one rather than another, when they are all alike and there is no reason to incline us to such a preference — answer that this movement of the soul is extraordinary and irregular, coming into us by some foreign, accidental, fortuitous impulse. It might rather, I think, be said that nothing presents itself to us in which there is not some difference, however slight; and that, either by sight or touch, there is always some choice which, however imperceptibly, tempts and attracts us. So whoever assumes a length of pack-thread of equal strength all the way through — it is simply impossible it should break, for where would you have the breaking to begin? And that it should break all at once is not in nature. Whoever should also throw in here the geometrical propositions which, by the certainty of their demonstrations, conclude the contained to be greater than the container, the centre to be as great as its circumference, and which discover two lines forever approaching each other and yet never able to meet — and the philosopher's stone, and the squaring of the circle, where reason and effect are so opposite — might perhaps find some argument to back up this bold saying of Pliny:
"Solum certum nihil esse certi, et homine nihil miserius aut superbius."
["It is only certain that nothing is certain, and that nothing is more miserable, or more proud, than man." — Nat. Hist., ii. 7.]
